spoken: A building has collapsed. The lights are out, there is no G P S, and radios barely reach through the walls.
Before anyone goes in, a team of small robots does.
Each robot builds its own map from two cameras and a motion sensor.
They share only what is worth the bytes, and they refuse look-alike places that would tear the shared map apart.
The estimation, mapping and planning are our own code, and every number we show links to a recorded run.
But a map is not a plan. Which opening should a robot check next, and why?
That is the job we gave to NVIDIA Nemotron, running on Nebius Token Factory.
The planner proposes candidate goals. Its most promising frontiers become open hypotheses: does this gap lead somewhere a person could follow?
On every replan, Nemotron reads the candidates and the open hypotheses through tool calls, and assigns each robot a goal. It can name the hypothesis that goal should test.
On screen: the Nemotron model that answered, and how long it took.
That choice is only a proposal. A plain C plus plus gate checks it is one of the planner's own candidates, used exactly once, and anything risky waits for a person to approve it.
Three things never come from the model.
A hypothesis's status comes from what the robots actually observed. Escape routes come from the planner, checked at forty centimetres, the width of a responder. And spending has a hard cap.
If the model fails, the robots carry on with the classical planner.
Robots that look for evidence before people go in.
Nemotron on Nebius chooses; observed geometry decides.
The code is open, under the M I T licence.
